title: Effect of intercritical annealing and subsequent ageing on the microstructure and mechanical properties of a medium Ni–Mn low carbon steel
abstract: The aim of this research was to develop a medium Ni–Mn dual phase steel with a combination of relatively high strength and good formability for industrial applications. Accordingly, this research was conducted to examine the effects of intercritical annealing and subsequent ageing treatments on the microstructure and mechanical properties of an Fe-9.5Ni-6.5Mn (wt.%) low carbon martensitic steel. Electron back scattering diffraction (EBSD) analysis revealed that intercritical annealing treatment at 610 °C in the ferrite + austenite (α+γ) dual phase region for various holding times led to formation of the reversed austenite phase in the martensite matrix, producing a medium Ni–Mn dual phase steel. It was resulted that the volume fraction of austenite and its grain size were significantly increased with increasing the holding time. Also, high resolution transmission electron microscope (HRTEM) images illustrated the formation of nano-sized θ-NiMn precipitates within the martensite phase after subsequent ageing at 450 °C for 7.2 ks. Intercritical annealing followed by ageing yielded a good combination of an ultimate tensile strength (∼1160 MPa) and fracture strain (∼11.5%) in the developed dual phase steel compared to the initial martensitic steel. The high strength and good ductility of the developed dual phase steel were respectively attributed to the presence of θ-NiMn precipitates with a hard character and reversely formed austenite with a ductile nature in the microstructure. Furthermore, the fully brittle fracture mode in the aged initial steel changed to a mixture of brittle and ductile behavior in the dual phase steel produced by intercritical annealing and subsequent ageing.
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Medium Ni–Mn low carbon steels are a suitable candidate for practical applications where ultra-strengths with a good level of formability are needed. These alloys are classified as high strength steels, which have the lath martensite microstructure accompanied by a high density of dislocations [ 1–3 ]. The microstructure of a fully lath martensitic steel consists of martensite lath, block, and packet. Martensite lath is a single crystal of martensite with a high density of lattice defects such as dislocations. The block is a variant of martensite that contains the laths with the same crystallographic orientation, and the packet consists of blocks that have the same plane of parent austenite [ 3–5 ].

Fe-9.5Ni-6.5Mn (wt.%) low carbon martensitic steel is sufficiently ductile in the solution-treated condition, but exhibits a brittle manner after subsequent ageing due to the formation of θ-NiMn precipitates. The main causes of embrittlement of this alloy after an ageing treatment are segregation of Mn atoms, precipitates formation and discontinuous coarsening of the precipitates at the prior austenite grain boundaries [ 6–9 ]. One of the promising ways for improving the mechanical properties of Fe–Ni–Mn steels is to apply the severe plastic deformation on the material. Recently, the effects of equal-channel angular pressing (ECAP) [ 10 ], heavy cold rolling [ 11–14 ], and high-pressure torsion (HPT) processing [ 15–18 ] on the mechanical properties of the present alloy have been investigated. In these processes, in addition to the grain refinement, the stress-induced austenite phase with a shear nature is partially formed in the martensite matrix and improves the mechanical behavior [ 11–15 ]. A prior intercritical annealing in ferritic + austenitic (α+γ) two-phase region is the other way to improve the mechanical properties of Fe–Ni–Mn steels after subsequent ageing. During this heat treatment, the reversely formed austenite with a ductile nature and appropriate grain size and morphology can be introduced in the martensite matrix and promotes the ductility of the material after subsequent ageing [ 19–24 ]. The reversely formed austenite during intercritical annealing has diffusional or diffusionless shear nature depending on the heating rate, annealing temperature, and holding time. Equiaxed and globular grains with a low density of dislocations are a characteristic of diffusional austenite, while lath-shaped reversed austenite with a high density of dislocation indicates the occurrence of diffusionless transformation [ 22–24 ].

Although some studies have been performed on the microstructural evolution of the Fe–Ni–Mn steels, it appears that the mechanical behavior of the intercritically annealed medium Ni–Mn low carbon steels has not been evaluated to date. It should be note that the subsequently aged Fe–Ni–Mn low carbon martensitic steels are very brittle and have no practical application. Therefore, the present study aims to investigate the effects of intercritical annealing and subsequent ageing treatments on the microstructure and mechanical behavior of an Fe–Ni–Mn martensitic alloy and to develop a dual phase medium Ni–Mn low carbon steel, which exhibits a combination of relatively high strength and good formability for industrial applications.

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs:
First, an ingot of Fe-9.5Ni-6.5Mn (wt.%) alloy was prepared by arc re-melting method under the protection of pure argon. The ingot was re-melted at least three times to achieve a proper homogeneity of chemical composition. The as-cast alloy was forged at 1150 °C to break the dendrites, and then homogenized at 1050 °C for 86.4 ks in a tube furnace under Argon gas atmosphere. Finally, the homogenized alloy was subjected to solution treatment at 900 °C for 7.2 ks and then quenched in water. Several samples were cut from the solution-treated (ST) ingot for the subsequent objects.  Table 1 
                          represents the chemical composition of the initial steel ingot after solution treatment.

sections.heading: Intercritical annealing and subsequent ageing treatments
paragraphs:
The ST samples were subjected to intercritical annealing in a salt bath at 610 °C in the ferritic + austenitic (α+γ) two phase region for 0.6, 1.2 and 3.6 ks holding times and then cooled to room temperature. Also, subsequent ageing treatment was done on the ST and intercritically annealed (IA) samples in a salt bath at 450 °C for 7.2 ks followed by cooling to room temperature. Previous reports represented that the austenite start (A s ) and finish (A f ) temperatures for the present alloy were respectively 570 and 640 °C, and also the precipitation start (P s ) and finish (P f ) temperatures were 380 and 480 °C, respectively [ 21 , 24 ]. Schematic representations of the heat treatment processes, including solution treatment, intercritical annealing and subsequent ageing, are shown in  Fig. 1 
                         .

sections.heading: Microstructural analysis
paragraphs: Microstructural characterization of the samples in various conditions was carried out using field-emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM), model Philips XL30S-FEG, equipped with an electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) system operating at 15 kV with a step size of 0.2 μm, and a high resolution transmission electron microscope (HRTEM), model PHILIPS CM200-FEG, operating at 200 kV. For EBSD observation, the samples were mechanically polished and then electroetched in a solution with a composition of 90% glacial acetic acid (CH 3 COOH) and 10% perchloric acid (HClO 4 ). For HRTEM analysis, disk-shaped samples were prepared by conventional twin-jet electropolishing of foils mechanically pre-thinned to 70 μm using an electrolyte of CrO 3 , CH 3 COOH and H 2 O at 10 °C and a voltage of 20–25 V.

sections.heading: Mechanical testing
paragraphs: Vickers microhardness (Hv) values for various samples were determined using a hardness machine with an applied load of 50 gf and a dwell time 0.01 ks. The average values reported for Hv were achieved from the average of five separate hardness values.

To evaluate the mechanical properties of the ST and IA specimens before and after ageing treatment, tensile testing was conducted at room temperature. For this purpose, the tensile specimens were cut from the various samples based on the ASTM  E8  standard with gauge dimensions of 25 × 6 × 2 mm 3  and examined by a SANTAM tensile machine with an initial strain rate of 5 × 10 −4  s −1 . In addition, the fracture surfaces of the tensile specimens were characterized using a FE-SEM.

sections.heading: Microstructural variations
paragraphs:
Fig. 2 
                         (a) shows the phase and grain boundary maps of the ST sample. The pink color region denotes the α′-martensite. In addition, the red lines indicate low-angle grain boundaries (LAGBs) with a misorientation angle between 2° and 15°, and the black lines correspond to the high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs) having the misorientation angle more than 15°. It is important to note that the LAGBs are indicative of the presence of dislocations in the microstructure [ 25 , 26 ]. From  Fig. 2 (a), it is clear that the microstructure of the ST sample is fully lath α′-martensite containing blocks and packets as a substructure of the lath martensite, accompanied by a high density of dislocations.  Fig. 2 (b) illustrates an orientation color map (inverse pole figure) of the ST sample, indicating a random distribution of the crystallographic directions of the martensite variants.

The phase and grain boundary maps as well as the orientation color maps (inverse pole figures) of the IA samples at 610 °C for different holding times are shown in  Fig. 3 
                         . According to the phase and grain boundary maps in  Fig. 3 (a), (c), and 3(e), the pink and green color regions denote the α′-martensite and γ-austenite phases, respectively. It is apparent that the grains of the austenite phase nucleate uniformly at the block and packet boundaries as well as at the grain boundaries of the martensite matrix, as previously reported [ 27 , 28 ], and the microstructures consist of α′-martensite and γ-austenite phases. In addition, it is obvious that the amount of retained austenite and its grain size increase with increasing holding time from 0.6 ( Fig. 3 (a)) to 3.6 ks ( Fig. 3 (e)). There is also a high amount of LAGBs in the austenite region, red lines in the austenite phase indicated by black circles in  Fig. 3 (a), (c), and (e), representing a high density of dislocations. This demonstrates that the reversely formed austenite inherits the dislocation structure (LAGBs) from the lath martensite. Furthermore, from the orientation color maps of the IA samples for different holding times ( Fig. 3 (b), (d), and (f)), it can be seen that there is a random distribution of the crystallographic directions of martensite and austenite phases.

Fig. 4 
                          shows the amounts of retained austenite in the martensite matrix at room temperature for the IA samples for various holding times. These values were obtained from the EBSD analyses. It is obvious that the volume fraction of retained austenite at room temperature in the IA sample for 0.6 ks is ∼15%, which increases with increasing holding time so that its value reaches ∼28% and ∼45% for the IA samples for 1.2 and 3.6 ks, respectively.

The amounts of LAGBs and HAGBs in the ST sample and IA samples for different holding times were resulted from EBSD analysis as indicated in  Fig. 5 
                         . It is obvious that the amount of LAGBs for the ST sample is ∼64% due to the presence of high density of dislocations in the lath martensitic microstructure. For the IA samples, the volume fraction of LAGBs in early stage of intercritical annealing (0.6 ks) is ∼48%, which decreases with increasing holding time so that its value reaches ∼23% for the IA sample for 3.6 ks. It can be said that the reduction in dislocation density caused by the recovery process is the main reason for the reduction in the amount of LAGBs.

Fig. 6 
                          exhibits the bright field HRTEM images of the ST sample and IA sample for 0.6 ks before and after subsequent ageing at 450 °C for 7.2 ks, as well as corresponding selected area electron diffraction (SAED) patterns obtained from the α′-martensite, γ-austenite and θ-NiMn precipitates. The ST sample shows typical lath α′-martensite with a high density of dislocation and an average lath thickness of about 150 nm ( Fig. 6 (a)). As shown in  Fig. 6 (b), after the ageing treatment of the ST sample, the θ-NiMn nano-particles precipitate in the martensite matrix. The SAED pattern of the microstructure proves the formation of precipitates in the lath α′-martensite.  Fig. 6 (c) shows the bright field HRTEM image of the IA sample for 0.6 ks, in which the lath-shaped austenite and martensite phases are denoted. The insets of Ι and ΙΙ in  Fig. 6 (c) respectively show the SAED patterns obtained from the martensite and austenite areas corresponding to the indexed spots of the bcc and fcc crystal structures. Accordingly, similar to the EBSD analysis, HRTEM observation confirms the formation of lath-shaped austenite with a high density of dislocations in the martensitic microstructure during intercritical annealing. Therefore, it can be concluded that austenite formation under intercritical annealing occurs by a diffusionless shear mechanism, as reported earliear [ 24 ]. Eventually,  Fig. 6 (d) shows the bright field HRTEM image of the IA sample for 0.6 ks followed by ageing. Based on the figure, it is noticeable that the precipitates formation only takes place in the α′-martensite region and there is no trace of them in the retained austenite.

sections.heading: Mechanical behavior
paragraphs:
Fig. 7 
                          represents the Vickers micro-hardness (Hv) results for the samples in the ST and IA conditions before and after subsequent ageing. Each recorded micro-hardness value represents the average of five different measurements. The micro-hardness value of the ST sample is ∼280 Hv, which increases significantly to ∼600 Hv after subsequent ageing. This increase in hardness value is due to the formation of nano-sized θ-NiMn precipitates with a hard and brittle nature. For the IA sample for 0.6 ks, the micro-hardness is ∼330 Hv, which is higher than that of the ST sample due to the shear-formed austenite with a high density of dislocations and a relatively fine grain size. By increasing the annealing time, the shear-formed austenite is recovered and its grains grow, so the micro-hardness decreases and reaches ∼290 Hv after a holding time of 3.6 ks. For the IA samples followed by ageing, the micro-hardness value is measured at ∼510 Hv for the sample annealed for 0.6 ks and decreases to ∼370 Hv for the sample annealed for 3.6 ks.

The engineering stress–strain curves at room temperature for the ST and the IA tensile specimens before and after the subsequent ageing treatment are shown in  Fig. 8 
                         . Also, the typical values of mechanical properties such as yield strength (YS), ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and fracture strain of the different specimens are listed in  Table 2 
                         . The values of UTS and fracture strain for the ST specimen are ∼710 MPa and ∼16.3%, respectively. After the subsequent ageing treatment of the ST specimen, the fracture strain significantly drops to ∼0.8% due to the formation of brittle and fine θ-NiMn precipitates. This indicates that the aged specimen has a purely brittle nature, so that it suddenly breaks in the elastic region when the applied stress is increased to about 1050 MPa. For the IA specimen for 0.6 ks, the UTS and fracture strain are respectively measured ∼780 MPa and ∼14.4%. The higher strength and lower elongation of the IA specimen compared to the ST one are related to the shear-formed austenite with a high density of dislocations and a relatively fine grain size. After subsequent ageing treatment of the IA specimen for 0.6 ks, the UTS increases meaningfully to ∼1420 MPa with a corresponding reduction in the fracture strain to ∼5.8% due to the precipitates formation in the microstructure. By increasing the prior intercritical annealing time to 1.2 and 3.6 ks in the subsequently aged-IA specimens, the UTS decreases to ∼1160 MPa and ∼870 MPa, and the fracture strain increases to ∼11.5% and ∼13.6%, respectively. This decrease in UTS and increase in the fracture strain are related to the increase of the amount of austenite and its grain growth with an increase in intercritical annealing time.

Fig. 9 
                          shows the FE-SEM images of the fracture surfaces of the ST and IA tensile specimens before and after subsequent ageing. It is apparent that there are significant differences in the fracture morphology of the aged and non-aged specimens. According to  Fig. 9 (a), the presence of dimples with various sizes and depths in the fracture surface proves the occurrence of an intragranular ductile fracture mode in the ST specimen. After the subsequent ageing treatment of the ST specimen ( Fig. 9 (b)), the broken tensile specimen exhibits intergranular fracture with predominant secondary cracks propagated along the grain boundaries, as indicated by arrows. These observations confirm the occurrence of a fully brittle facture mode. The cleavage features of brittle fracture are also present in this specimen [ 29 ]. As shown in  Fig. 9 (c), the fracture surface of the IA specimen for 0.6 ks displays similar dimples as the ST specimen, but with smaller sizes, suggesting a ductile fracture mode. For the subsequently aged-IA specimen for 0.6 ks ( Fig. 9 (d)), there is a mixture of intragranular fine dimples and the some cracks propagated along the grain boundaries in the fractography of specimen, suggesting a combination of intragranular ductile and intergranular brittle fracture modes. By increasing the prior intercritical annealing time to 1.2 ks in the subsequently aged-IA specimen, the fraction of the dimples in the fracture surface increases and the specimen shows a relatively soft nature ( Fig. 9 (e)). Finally, as indicated in  Fig. 9 (f), the fractography of the IA specimen for 3.6 ks followed by ageing shows only dimples, demonstrating a fully ductile fracture mode.

sections.heading: Microstructural variations
paragraphs: It is resulted from the EBSD map in  Fig. 2  (a) that the ST sample has a fully lath martensitic microstructure with a high fraction of LAGBs. The high amount of LAGBs is related to the high density of dislocations in the microstructure. Lath in the martensitic steels is a single crystal of martensite with a high density of dislocations and lattice defects [ 3–5 ]. During intercritical annealing of the ST sample in ferritic + austenitic (α+γ) two phase region, the reverse transformation of martensite to austenite (α′→γ) takes place, and the austenite phase with a high density of dislocations nucleates uniformly in the martensite matrix so that its grain size increases with increasing annealing time ( Fig. 3 ). Also, as indicated in  Figs. 3  and  4 , the volume fraction of the retained austenite at room temperature increases from ∼15% to ∼45% when the holding time is increased from 0.6 to 3.6 ks.

Based on the HRTEM images in  Fig. 6  (a), it is obvious that the microstructure of the ST specimen is a fully lath α′-martensite with a high density of dislocations. During intercritical annealing ( Fig. 6 (c)), the microstructure is refined and the lath-shaped reversed austenite with a high density of dislocations is introduced in the martensitic matrix. The presence of high density of dislocations in the austenite phase indicates that the dislocation structure is inherited from the martensite to the reversely formed austenite. This observation confirms that the reverse transformation of the martensite to austenite occurs by a diffusionless shear mechanism. Previous researches reported that the lath-shaped austenite with a high density of dislocation was a production of a diffusionless shear transformation [ 22–24 ]. From  Fig. 6 (b) and (d), it is revealed that the formation of θ-NiMn precipitates in the ST and IA samples after subsequent ageing occurs only in the martensite phase and no trace of it is found in the retained austenite region. This is related to the super-saturated nature of the martensite matrix in terms of chemical composition [ 6 , 9 , 30 , 31 ].

sections.heading: Mechanical behavior
paragraphs: According to the micro-hardness results in  Fig. 7 , the EBSD maps in  Fig. 3  and HRTEM images in  Fig. 6 , it is anticipated that the higher micro-hardness value of the IA sample for 0.6 ks (∼330 Hv) compared to the ST one (∼280 Hv) is due to the formation of diffusionless shear austenite with a high density of dislocations and a relatively fine grain size. By increasing intercritical annealing time, the micro-hardness gradually decreases and reaches a value of ∼290 Hv in the IA sample for 3.6 ks, which can be attributed to the recovery process in the shear-formed austenite and its subsequent grain growth [ 22 , 24 ]. A significant increase in the micro-hardness value of the aged-ST sample (∼600 Hv) and the aged-IA sample for 0.6 ks (∼510 Hv) is related to the formation of nano-sized θ-NiMn precipitates with a hard nature. Since the precipitation takes place only in the martensite phase [ 6 , 9 , 30 ], the micro-hardness value of the aged-IA sample for 0.6 ks is lower than that of the aged-ST sample. In addition, since the volume fraction of retained austenite increases with increasing intercritical annealing time, the micro-hardness values of the aged-IA samples decrease.

As indicated in  Fig. 8  and presented in  Table 2 , for the ST specimen, the values of YS and UTS are very close together and there is only a minor strain hardening due to the presence of high density of dislocations in the lath martensite. However, the specimen has a considerable post-uniform deformation after necking, which is due to the relatively ductile nature of the lath-martensite matrix. Fracture strain for this specimen is ∼16.3%. After the subsequent ageing treatment of the ST specimen, the ductility of alloy drastically drops and the sample suddenly breaks in the elastic region. This indicates that the aged-ST specimen is very brittle due to the θ-NiMn precipitates formation and there has insignificant practical applications. Intercritical annealing of the ST specimen for 0.6 ks enhances the UTS value to ∼780 MPa and simultaneously decreases its fracture strain to ∼14.4%. The higher strength and lower elongation of the IA specimen for 0.6 ks compared to the ST specimen are associated with the shear-formed austenite with a high density of dislocations and a relatively fine grain size. After subsequent ageing treatment of the IA specimen for 0.6 ks, the UTS increases significantly to ∼1420 MPa with a corresponding reduction in the fracture strain to ∼5.8% by strengthening the microstructure through the formation of θ-NiMn precipitates. An increase in the prior intercritical annealing time leads to a decrease in the UTS value and an increase in the fracture strain in the aged-IA specimens, which is attributed to increase of the amount of austenite and its grain growth with an increase in the intercritical annealing time [ 22 , 24 ]. Accordingly, an outstandingly good combination of UTS (∼1160 MPa) and fracture strain (∼11.5%) achieves for the aged-IA specimen for 1.2 ks. It is important to note that by contrast to the ST specimen, the tensile test results of the IA specimens before and after subsequent ageing show a pre-uniform deformation before necking. This difference is attributed to the bi-modal microstructure of the specimens which includes a high volume fraction of ductile austenite and a high dislocation martensite.

The FE-SEM micrographs of the fracture surfaces in  Fig. 9  confirm the results of the tensile test. According to  Fig. 9 (a), the ductile fracture surface of the ST tensile specimen is in good agreement with the obtained elongation of ∼16.3%. For the aged-ST specimen ( Fig. 9 (b)), the fracture behavior changes from the fully ductile to purely brittle due to the formation of θ-NiMn precipitates, so that the fracture surface indicates intergranular fracture with prevailing secondary cracks propagated along the grain boundaries. Also, the quasi-cleavage fracture in this specimen is the result of fine precipitates and grain boundary fracture that occurred after aging heat treatment [ 10 , 29 ]. The fracture surface of the IA specimen for 0.6 ks shows dimple morphology with a smaller size than that of the ST specimen, indicating the occurrence of a ductile fracture mode ( Fig. 9 (c)). The refinement of the microstructure and the formation of diffusionless shear austenite under intercritical annealing are the main reasons for the smaller dimples formation in the IA specimen compared to the ST specimen. As indicated in  Fig. 9 (d), there is a mixture of fine intragranular dimples and some cracks propagated along the grain boundaries in the fracture surface of the aged-IA specimen for 0.6 ks, indicating a combination of ductile and brittle fracture modes. The ductile nature of the dual phase specimen is due to the presence of the austenite phase, while its brittle nature is related to the formation of θ-NiMn precipitates in the martensite matrix. Increasing the prior intercritical annealing time leads to the development of the dimple morphology in the fracture surface of the subsequently aged specimens, so that a fully ductile fracture mode is observed for the aged-IA specimen for 3.6 ks. This ductile behavior is due to the increase of the amount of retained austenite in the lath-martensite matrix and its grain growth by increasing the annealing time.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs:
Experiments were conducted to evaluate the effects of intercritical annealing and subsequent ageing treatments on the microstructure and mechanical behavior of an Fe-9.5Ni-6.5Mn (wt.%) low carbon martensitic steel in the ST condition. The results led to the following conclusions: 
                         
                            1. 
                            EBSD and HRTEM results indicated that during the intercritical annealing of the ST sample, the lath-shaped austenite with a high density of dislocations was nucleated in the martensite microstructure by a diffusionless shear mechanism, resulting in the development of a medium Ni–Mn dual phase steel. 
                         
                         
                            2. 
                            Experimental results represented that the volume fraction of retained austenite at room temperature in the IA sample for 0.6 ks was ∼15%, which increased with increasing holding time so that its value reached ∼28% and ∼45% for the IA samples for 1.2 and 3.6 ks, respectively. Additionally, the grain size of austenite was significantly increased by increasing the intercritical annealing time. 
                         
                         
                            3. 
                            HRTEM images showed that the subsequent ageing treatment of the ST and IA samples introduced fine θ-NiMn precipitates in the martensite matrix. 
                         
                         
                            4. 
                            Subsequent ageing treatment of the IA specimen for 0.6 ks yielded an outstandingly good combination of an UTS (∼1160 MPa) and fracture strain (∼11.5%) in the developed dual phase steel compared to the ST steel with a fully lath martensitic microstructure. This could be attributed to the presence of hard precipitates and reversely formed austenite with a ductile nature in the microstructure. 
                         
                         
                            5. 
                            The tensile test results confirmed that the fully brittle fracture mode in the aged initial steel changed to a combination of ductile and brittle character, accompanied by a good mechanical behavior in the dual phase steel developed by intercritical annealing and subsequent ageing treatments.

sections.heading: Data availability
paragraphs: The raw/processed data required to reproduce these findings cannot be shared at this time as the data form part of an ongoing study.
